Review draft. This chapter has a source-specific comparison, complete worked bank, final examination decisions and compact geometric laboratories. Its recorded audits describe the checks performed; student approval is separate. It follows Orthogonality and Orthogonal Decompositions and precedes Least Squares and Applications.

1. Written sources and the purpose of this chapter

The core synthesis uses MIT 18.06 SC Session 2.3, Stanford EE 263 Lecture 5, Oxford M1 Linear Algebra I (metric and adjoint foundations), and Berkeley Math 54 Orthogonal Projections. ETH Zurich's Linear Algebra PartII supplies an additional precise QR argument. Exact reading ranges, conventions and the completed bounded comparison are in the source audit. Four university names do not substitute for a documented chapter-specific selection.

The prerequisite chapter established inner products and the existence of perpendicular decompositions. Here the object of study is the projection operator itself: how to construct it from imperfectly presented generators, identify it from algebraic conditions, recognize its range and kernel, calculate distances, combine it with other projections, and distinguish physical vectors from their coordinates. An examination question may never mention geometry; it may give an idempotent matrix, a trace identity, an affine constraint or an unfamiliar weighted product. The same operator must be recognized through all these representations.

Unless otherwise declared, vectors are columns, the ambient space is finite dimensional, and real Euclidean geometry is used. Complex formulas use the conjugate transpose, written A*. The residual convention is always data minus projected data:

p=Pb,r=b-p=(I-P)b.

Stanford Lecture 5 instead writes the opposite residual. Its orthogonality conclusion is unchanged, but the sign of a displayed residual vector must be translated. Norm notation uses a complete grouped base before an exponent; a closing delimiter is not the base of the exponent.

2. A subspace and its generators are different objects

Let A∈ℝm×n and let S=Col(A). The subspace is a set of physical vectors in ℝm. A coefficient vector belongs to ℝn. Their dimensions and their roles differ:

c∈ℝn,Ac∈S⊆ℝm.

Repeating a generator, rescaling a nonzero generator, or adding a linear combination of earlier generators may change A and its coefficient descriptions without changing S. Therefore a formula for the physical projection should depend on S, not on a particular generator list. This requirement is an immediate diagnostic: an alleged projection formula that changes when a column is doubled is suspect.

An independent column basis C can be selected from A by identifying pivot columns of the original matrix. Row reduction discovers the indices; the basis vectors must be taken from the original columns. Substituting the corresponding columns of the row-reduced matrix usually changes the physical subspace. If the rank is zero, the subspace is the zero subspace and its projection is the zero operator. No empty inverse is needed.

3. The closest-point theorem, with existence and uniqueness separated

Choose an orthonormal basis q1,…,qk of S. Define

p=∑j=1kqj(qjTb),r=b-p.

For each basis vector, qiTr=qiTb-qiTb=0. By linearity, r is perpendicular to every vector in S. Thus a decomposition exists. For any candidate s∈S, the vector p-s is also in S, so it is perpendicular to r. Consequently

b-s=r+(p-s),‖b-s‖2=‖r‖2+‖p-s‖2.

The second term is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when s=p. This proves both optimality and uniqueness. The proof uses positive definiteness. A bilinear form that admits a nonzero vector of zero self-product does not support this uniqueness argument.

The theorem gives a practical certificate without optimization or inversion: a candidate p is the closest point exactly when p∈S and b-p∈S⊥. Checking only the dot product pT(b-p)=0 is insufficient. It tests one vector in the subspace, rather than every generator direction.

Closest point and its perpendicular residual

4. Linearity follows from the decomposition certificate

Suppose bi=pi+ri with pi∈S and ri∈S⊥. For scalars α,β, the decomposition of αb1+βb2 is

αb1+βb2=(αp1+βp2)+(αr1+βr2).

The first part belongs to S and the second to S⊥. Uniqueness therefore implies P(αb1+βb2)=αPb1+βPb2. This establishes linearity before a matrix formula is guessed.

The operator fixes every vector already in S and kills every vector in S⊥. Hence

P2=P,Range(P)=S,Ker(P)=S⊥.

The residual operator I-P projects onto S⊥. It is not an unrelated error-processing device: it is the complementary projection, and P(I-P)=(I-P)P=0.

5. Deriving the generator formula instead of memorizing it

Let C∈ℝm×k have independent columns and span S. Write p=Cc. Perpendicularity to every column gives

CT(b-Cc)=0,CTCc=CTb.

Why may the Gram matrix be inverted? For every nonzero z∈ℝk,

zTCTCz=‖Cz‖2>0.

The strict inequality follows from column independence. Thus CTC is positive definite, and

c=(CTC)-1CTb,P=C(CTC)-1CT.

The dimensions are m×k, k×k, and k×m; their product is an m×m ambient operator. Reversing a transpose can produce a dimensionally meaningless expression even when the source page appears authoritative.

If C is replaced by CR, where R is an invertible k×k matrix, the middle inverse becomes R-1(CTC)-1R-T. Multiplication cancels both changes, leaving exactly the same P. This is a constructive proof of basis invariance. Coefficients change to R-1c; the physical vector does not.

6. Worked problem: a plane with a hidden normal

Let the plane be generated by a1=(1,0,1)T and a2=(0,1,1)T, and project b=(1,2,0)T. The generator matrix and its Gram system are

C=(100111),CTC=(2112),CTb=(12).

The inverse Gram matrix is one third of (2-1-12). Therefore c=(0,1)T, p=(0,1,1)T, and r=(1,1,-1)T. Both generator products with r vanish. The squared distance is 3; the norm decomposition reads 5=2+3.

There is a second derivation. A normal is n=(-1,-1,1)T, so S=n⊥ and

P=I-nnTnTn=13(2-11-121112).

Applying this matrix yields the same p. The two derivations cross-check the signs of the normal and the distinction between projection onto the plane and projection onto its normal line. Changing n to -n leaves the outer product unchanged.

7. Dependent generators: unique vector, nonunique coefficients

Add a3=a1+a2 to the preceding generator list. The new three-column matrix has rank two, so ATA is singular. Its column space and its orthogonal projector are unchanged. All coefficient descriptions of the projected vector satisfy

c1+c3=0,c2+c3=1.

Thus every coefficient vector has the form c=(-t,1-t,t)T. Every such vector maps to the same p. A normal-equation solution alone does not guarantee a unique coefficient vector.

To select the minimum Euclidean coefficient norm, minimize t2+(1-t)2+t2=3t2-2t+1. Completing the square gives

3t2-2t+1=3(t-13)2+23.

The unique minimum-norm coefficient vector is (-1/3,2/3,1/3)T. It is perpendicular to the coefficient nullspace generated by (-1,-1,1)T. This is a statement in coefficient space; it must not be confused with the observation residual r=(1,1,-1)T in the ambient space, despite the coincident dimensions in this particular example.

A pseudoinverse may express this selection as c=A+b. The operator AA+ is the orthogonal projection onto the column space. Defining or deriving A+ correctly is essential: the full-column-rank formula cannot simply be applied to a dependent matrix.

8. Rectangular orthonormal bases and the QR route

If Q∈ℝm×k has orthonormal columns, then QTQ=Ik and the projector is QQT. Unless k=m, the reverse product is not the ambient identity. It is a rank- k projection.

For a full-column-rank factorization C=QR with invertible triangular R, substitute into the generator formula. The middle inverse is R-1R-T; cancellation gives

C(CTC)-1CT=QQT.

To apply the projector, first measure the orthonormal coordinates QTb and then reconstruct Q(QTb). This uses neither an explicit Gram inverse nor an ambient dense matrix. If a full orthogonal matrix is partitioned as [Q1Q2] with Q1 spanning S, then P=Q1Q1T, I-P=Q2Q2T, and the squared distance is ‖Q2Tb‖2.

For computation, solving a triangular system is preferable to explicitly forming its inverse. The exact formulas establish mathematics; a numerically stable algorithm requires an additional conditioning discussion.

9. Algebraic recognition: symmetry and idempotence together

An orthogonal projector is symmetric and idempotent. Conversely, suppose a real square matrix satisfies PT=P and P2=P. Every x decomposes as Px+(I-P)x. The first component lies in the range. For any range vector Py,

(Py)T(I-P)x=yTP(I-P)x=0.

The second component is perpendicular to the whole range. The closest-point theorem therefore identifies P as its orthogonal projection. This proves the characterization without assuming a spectral theorem.

Idempotence alone only gives a direct-sum decomposition into range and kernel. For E=(1200), E2=E, but the vertical unit vector maps to (2,0)T. Length increases from one to two. Its residual follows the oblique kernel, not the Euclidean perpendicular direction.

Symmetry alone also fails. The diagonal matrix with entries 2 and 0 is symmetric but doubles the first coordinate. Checking only trace, rank or determinant never replaces both defining identities.

An oblique idempotent is not a closest-point map

10. Contraction characterizes an idempotent projection

Every orthogonal projector satisfies ‖Px‖≤‖x‖ by Pythagoras. Conversely, suppose P2=P and P contracts every vector. Let u lie in the range and v in the kernel. Then P(u+tv)=u for every real t, so

‖u‖2≤‖u+tv‖2=‖u‖2+2tuTv+t2‖v‖2.

If uTv were nonzero, choosing t=-uTv/‖v‖2 would make the right-hand difference negative. Therefore range and kernel are perpendicular. The idempotent is orthogonal. The zero-kernel or zero-vector cases require no division and already satisfy the conclusion.

Testing contraction on a single vector is insufficient. The quantifier is every vector. This proof also explains how an oblique projector necessarily expands some input: a kernel component can partly cancel a range component before the oblique projection removes it.

11. Rank, trace, spectrum and the operator norm

If Pv=λv for a nonzero vector, idempotence implies λ2=λ, so an eigenvalue is zero or one. More strongly, an idempotent is diagonalizable even when it is oblique: choose a basis of its range followed by a basis of its kernel. Their intersection is zero, and every vector splits into both parts. The matrix in that basis is diag(Ik,0).

It follows that the rank and trace equal k. The determinant is zero unless the rank is the full ambient dimension, in which case idempotence forces P=I. Trace equals rank for oblique idempotents as well; it does not certify symmetry.

For an orthogonal projector, xTPx=‖Px‖2≥0, and the same is true for I-P. Thus its quadratic form lies between zero and xTx. Its operator norm is one if the range is nonzero, since a nonzero range vector is fixed. The zero projector has norm zero. Its squared Frobenius norm equals tr(PTP)=tr(P)=k.

12. Diagonal entries and hidden coordinate information

For the standard unit vector ei, the diagonal entry is pii=eiTPei=‖Pei‖2. Consequently 0≤pii≤1 and the diagonal sum equals the rank. Symmetry and idempotence also give

∑jpij2=pii.

If pii=0, the whole corresponding row and column vanish. If pii=1, the diagonal square already exhausts the row's squared norm, so every off-diagonal entry in that row is zero; the coordinate direction belongs to the range.

Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to Pei and Pej. Since their product is pij,

pij2≤piipjj.

Applying the same argument to I-P gives pij2≤(1-pii)(1-pjj) when i≠j. These inequalities are useful necessary tests, but a candidate matrix satisfying them need not be a projector. The identities P2=P and PT=P remain decisive.

13. Weighted geometry: the operator may look nonsymmetric

Let G be real symmetric positive definite and define the product xTGy. The projection onto an independent column basis C is

PG=C(CTGC)-1CTG.

The proof repeats the membership and perpendicular-residual certificate, now with CTG(b-PGb)=0. The Gram matrix remains positive definite because Cz is nonzero for nonzero z. The operator is idempotent but generally not symmetric in ordinary coordinates. Its correct self-adjointness identity is PGTG=GPG.

For G=diag(1,4) and C=(1,1)T,

PG=15(1414).

For b=(2,0)T, the projection is (2/5,2/5)T and the residual is (8/5,-2/5)T. Their weighted product is zero. The squared input norm is 4, the squared projected norm is 4/5, and the squared residual norm is 16/5. Ordinary symmetry is absent; weighted orthogonality is exact.

Writing G=LTL with invertible L converts physical vectors to Euclidean coordinates y=Lx. The transformed projector LPGL-1 is Euclidean orthogonal. This is a change of metric representation, not permission to substitute ordinary transpose for the weighted adjoint.

Weighted projection: coordinate angles can mislead

14. Complex vectors require conjugation

For a complex column basis, replace each transpose in the Euclidean construction by conjugate transpose:

P=C(C*C)-1C*.

For c=(1,i)T, the squared norm is c*c=2 and

P=12(1-ii1).

Projecting b=(1,0)T gives p=(1/2,i/2)T and r=(1/2,-i/2)T. The conjugate product c*r is zero and P*=P. Using cTc would give zero for a nonzero generator and falsely suggest that its Gram matrix is singular. This is a convention error, not a failure of the projection theorem.

15. Affine spaces: translate, project, and translate back

An affine space has the form a+S. To find its closest point to b, minimize the distance from b-a to S. The result is

Πa+S(b)=a+P(b-a)=Pb+(I-P)a.

Changing the representative a by a vector in S leaves the constant term unchanged. The mapping is affine and idempotent, but generally not linear. It is linear exactly when (I-P)a=0, which means the affine space contains the origin and is the same subspace S.

For a hyperplane nTx=d with nonzero normal n, the closest point is

p=b-nnTb-dnTn.

Take n=(1,2,-1)T, d=3, and b=(2,0,1)T. The violation is -2, so p=b+n/3=(7/3,2/3,2/3)T. Direct substitution gives nTp=3. The correction has squared length 2/3, which is also the squared distance to the hyperplane. This squared distance differs from the squared distance to the parallel subspace through the origin.

A two-dimensional affine analogue

16. Several affine constraints and their qualifications

Let D have independent rows and impose Dx=d. The kernel of D is the direction subspace. A correction perpendicular to it belongs to the row space, so write p=b-DTλ. The constraints imply DDTλ=Db-d, giving

p=b-DT(DDT)-1(Db-d).

For D=(110011), d=(1,2)T and b=0, the Gram inverse yields the closest feasible point p=(0,1,1)T. Its squared norm is two. The direction kernel is generated by (-1,1,-1)T, whose dot product with p is zero. This checks both feasibility and minimal norm.

Dependent rows require two separate checks: consistency of the affine constraints and a valid inverse or pseudoinverse on the independent row space. A dependent but consistent system has a unique closest feasible vector. An inconsistent system has no point to project onto; solving a least-squares surrogate changes the question.

17. Combining projectors: commutation is a substantive hypothesis

Let P,Q be orthogonal projectors. If they commute, then PQ is symmetric and idempotent. Its range equals the intersection of their ranges: an output PQx is fixed by both, while a vector fixed by both is fixed by PQ. Therefore PQ projects onto that intersection.

Conversely, if PQ is an orthogonal projector, symmetry gives PQ=(PQ)T=QP. The condition is necessary as well as sufficient. A product of projections is not automatically a projection.

For projection onto the horizontal axis and onto the line generated by (1,1)T,

P=(1000),Q=12(1111),PQ=12(1100).

The product is neither symmetric nor idempotent. Repeated application multiplies its nonzero part by one half each time. The intersection is the zero subspace, so repeated products tend toward its zero projection, but a single product is not that limit. A simulation must show the actual finite iterates rather than label every intermediate result as an intersection projection.

Finite alternating projection cycles

18. Sums, differences and contained subspaces

If the ranges are perpendicular, then PQ=QP=0 and P+Q is the projection onto their orthogonal direct sum. Conversely, idempotence of P+Q gives PQ+QP=0. Taking trace yields 2tr(PQ)=0. For orthogonal projectors,

tr(PQ)=‖PQ‖F2≥0.

Thus PQ=0, proving necessity. The argument uses symmetry; it must not be transplanted without qualification to arbitrary oblique idempotents.

If the range of P is contained in the range of Q, then QP=P and, by transpose, PQ=P. The difference Q-P is an orthogonal projector onto the part of the larger range perpendicular to the smaller range. The sign matters: P-Q then has eigenvalue minus one on that removed part, so it is generally not a projector.

19. Measuring how different two projections are

For ranks r and s, expand the Frobenius square using symmetry and idempotence:

‖P-Q‖F2=r+s-2tr(PQ).

The trace is nonnegative by the preceding identity. It is at most both ranks: applying the contraction of Q to an orthonormal basis of the range of P shows that the sum of squared projected lengths is at most r, and the reverse argument gives s.

If the intersection has dimension t, extend an orthonormal basis of the intersection to a basis of the range of P. Each intersection vector contributes one to that same trace sum; every other contribution is nonnegative. Hence the trace is at least t, and t≥r+s-m when the ambient dimension is m. In particular

max(0,r+s-m)≤tr(PQ)≤min(r,s).

The trace is usually not the dimension of the intersection. For two distinct nonperpendicular lines in a plane, the intersection has dimension zero while the trace equals the squared cosine of their angle and is positive. This gives an immediate conceptual counterexample to a tempting rank formula.

20. Rank changes and a discontinuous limiting projection

Let Aε=(110ε). For every nonzero ε, its columns span the full plane and its orthogonal projector is the identity. At ε=0, they span only the horizontal line, whose projector is diag(1,0).

Thus the matrices of generators converge while their associated projection matrices do not converge to the projection of the limiting range. The rank changes at the limit. For the target (0,1)T, exact coefficients at nonzero ε are (-1/ε,1/ε)T: the physical fitted vector remains fixed while the coefficient magnitude diverges.

This example separates three statements: the projection is well-defined at every parameter value, coefficient recovery can be ill-conditioned near dependent columns, and continuity of a projection as a function of its generators requires a fixed-rank qualification. Treating a very small nonzero parameter as exactly zero without declaring a numerical rank policy changes the subspace.

21. Reflection is reversible; projection discards information

Let P be the Euclidean orthogonal projector onto S. Define the reflection that fixes S by H=2P-I. If x=s+n is its perpendicular decomposition, then Hx=s-n. Therefore H preserves the component parallel to the reflecting subspace and reverses the perpendicular component. Applying it twice returns x. Algebraically,

HT=H,H2=4P2-4P+I=I,HTH=I.

Thus this reflection is both symmetric and orthogonal, although P is usually not an orthogonal matrix. An orthogonal projection is a closest-point map; an orthogonal matrix preserves every norm. A matrix can have the former description without the latter. Only the full-space orthogonal projector P=I is also an invertible orthogonal matrix.

For a nonzero normal n, projection onto n⊥ gives P=I-nnT/(nTn). Its reflection is

H=I-2nnTnTn.

The normal direction has eigenvalue minus one, and each direction in the hyperplane has eigenvalue one. More generally, the reflection fixing a rank- k subspace in ℝm has determinant (-1)m-k and trace 2k-m. Conversely, if a real matrix is symmetric and orthogonal, then H2=I, and (I+H)/2 is its orthogonal projector onto the fixed space. Orthogonality without symmetry is insufficient: a general rotation need not give an idempotent average with the identity.

22. Change of coordinates also changes the metric

Let B be an invertible matrix whose columns are a coordinate basis, with physical vector x=Bz. If the physical projector is P, its coordinate matrix is E=B-1PB. Similarity preserves idempotence, rank and eigenvalues. Ordinary symmetry need not survive because the new basis need not be orthonormal.

The Euclidean physical squared length becomes zTBTBz. Set G=BTB. A correct coordinate representation satisfies

E2=E,ETG=GE.

To verify the second identity, substitute E=B-1PB and G=BTB. Both sides reduce to BTPB, using PT=P. Conversely, these identities make BEB-1 a physical Euclidean orthogonal projector. The metric carries the geometry that a nonorthonormal coordinate chart hides.

For B=(1101) and physical horizontal projector P=diag(1,0), the coordinate matrix is E=(1100). Its nonsymmetry does not imply that the physical map is oblique: coordinates use G=(1112). In the ordinary coordinate dot product, however, the same numerical matrix is an oblique projector. An examination must specify which metric is being used.

23. Alternating projections: derive the finite iterate first

Take the horizontal line and a line with unit direction u=(cosθ,sinθ)T. Write c=cosθ and s=sinθ, with 0<θ<π/2. Project first onto the sloping line by Q=uuT, then onto the horizontal line by P. One full cycle is

M=PQ=(c2cs00).

Multiplication gives M2=c2M, and induction gives

Mj=c2j-2M(j≥1).

The lines have zero intersection, so their intersection projector is zero. Since 0<c2<1, the finite iterates converge to zero. They are generally nonzero at every finite cycle. In particular, starting at e1, the output after j full cycles is c2je1. The error target c2j≤ε, for 0<ε<1, requires

j≥logε2logc.

Both logarithms are negative, so dividing by 2logc reverses the preceding logarithmic inequality. The least integer is the ceiling of the displayed quantity. At perpendicular lines, c=0 and one cycle is exact; at coincident lines, c=1 and the intersection is the whole line instead of zero. Neither endpoint belongs in the logarithmic formula. Nearly parallel distinct lines converge slowly, although every individual projection is norm nonincreasing.

For general finite-dimensional subspaces, the convergence statement also holds. One proof avoids assuming simultaneous diagonalization. Put T=S∩U. Both projectors fix T and preserve T⊥, since for t∈T and x⊥T, ⟨Px,t⟩=⟨x,Pt⟩=0. On T⊥, a nonzero vector cannot retain its norm through both projections: equality in each contraction would place it in both subspaces and hence in T. The continuous function x↦‖PQx‖ has a maximum ρ<1 on the unit sphere of T⊥, which is compact. Thus the error after j cycles is at most ρj times the initial perpendicular component. If T⊥ has dimension zero, both projections are the identity and the assertion is immediate. This proof uses finite dimension; infinite-dimensional analogues require different arguments and may lack a uniform rate.

24. Computing without constructing a dense projector

Suppose an m×k thin orthonormal basis Q is already available. Computing y=QTb uses mk scalar products and computing p=Qy uses another mk products, with comparable additions. Storage for Q is mk numbers. Building an m×m matrix QQT uses much more storage when k≪m and is unnecessary for a single target.

The following pseudocode emphasizes the dimensions and the required input contract. It assumes a previously verified orthonormal basis; it does not turn arbitrary generators into one.

project_with_basis(Q[m,k], b[m]):
    require transpose(Q) * Q = identity(k)
    y[k] = transpose(Q) * b
    p[m] = Q * y
    r[m] = b - p
    return p, r, dot(r,r)

For full-column-rank generators C=QR, coefficient recovery solves Rc=QTb by back substitution. The physical projection is Q(QTb) regardless of the conditioning of that coefficient recovery. If σmax and σmin are the largest and smallest positive singular values of C, then the eigenvalues of CTC are their squares. Therefore

κ2(CTC)=σmax2σmin2=κ2(C)2.

This exact identity explains why forming normal equations can amplify sensitivity in numerical coefficient calculations. It does not mean that every coefficient error is squared, that QR cures an intrinsically ill-conditioned problem, or that a dependent matrix has a finite full-column-rank condition number. Householder QR is a standard stable route for independent columns; rank-deficient numerical problems need a declared rank threshold, rank-revealing factorization or SVD. Exact arithmetic in the laboratory avoids rounding and does not certify arbitrary floating-point implementations.

25. Coverage map and boundaries

The core objectives are membership and perpendicularity certificates; basis construction and invariance; dependent coordinates; recognition by symmetry and idempotence; contraction; range, kernel, trace and diagonal constraints; weighted and complex geometry; affine feasibility; sums, products, containment and differences; trace overlap; reflection; coordinate change; finite iteration; and computational qualifications. The worked bank revisits these objectives through calculations, proofs and counterexamples. Basic checkpoints are deliberately interleaved with medium and hard synthesis so that a wrong hypothesis can be identified before a long calculation.

Detailed regression, random-noise estimation, pseudoinverse/SVD construction and statistical model selection belong to later chapters. This chapter uses or derives only the pseudoinverse examples needed to distinguish coefficient nonuniqueness from physical uniqueness. The sources were selected from a documented seven-university pool, not from an exhaustively searchable universe of all courses. Neither a finite source review nor a mathematical audit can guarantee perfect performance on every unseen examination question. The audit names what was checked and what remains uncertain.

Reflection fixes the line and reverses the residual

Fifty worked mathematical and conceptual problems

Problem 1. Build one plane projector by two independent routes

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Let S be spanned by (1,0,1) and (0,1,1). Find its orthogonal projection matrix, the projection of b=(2,1,0), and the squared distance from b to S. Explain why the closest point is unique.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Put the generators into the columns of

A=[100111],ATA=[2112].

The determinant of the Gram matrix is three, so the independent-column formula applies. Its inverse is one third of the matrix with diagonal two and off-diagonal negative one. Multiplication gives

P=A(ATA)-1AT=13[2-11-121112].

A normal to S is n=(−1,−1,1), since its dot product with either generator is zero. Its squared length is three, so the complementary route gives P=I-nnT/3, reproducing every entry above. This agreement checks both the subspace and the dimensions of the construction.

The projected point is p=(1,0,1), and the residual is r=b−p=(1,1,−1)=−n. The point p belongs to S; its coefficients in the displayed basis are (1,0). The residual is perpendicular to both generators. Thus ‖r‖2=3 is the squared distance. For any other s in S, the decomposition b−s=r+(p−s) has perpendicular terms, so its squared norm is three plus ‖p-s‖2. Equality occurs only at s=p, proving uniqueness. Checking only that p and r have zero dot product would be weaker: the residual must be perpendicular to the entire subspace.

Finite geometry for this problem

Problem 2. Dependent generators do not destroy a unique projection

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Let A have columns u=(1,2,0) and 2 u. For b=(2,1,3), determine the projection, all coefficient vectors producing it, and the minimum-norm coefficient vector. Explain why directly inverting A transpose A is invalid.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Both columns describe the same line S. Its projector depends on u, not on how often u is listed:

P=uuTuTu=15[120240000].

Here u transpose b is four. Hence p=(4/5,8/5,0)T and r=(6/5,-3/5,3)T. The residual satisfies u transpose r=0, and its squared norm is 36/25+9/25+9=54/5. The projection is unique by the closest-point theorem.

Coefficients c satisfy Ac=u(c1+2c2), so the full coefficient family is c1+2c2=4/5. Writing c₂=t gives c₁=4/5−2 t. The squared coefficient norm is (4/5-2t)2+t2. Completing the square, or differentiating this exact quadratic, gives t=8/25 and c₁=4/25. Thus the minimum-norm coefficient vector is (4/25,8/25), while infinitely many other coefficient vectors produce the same physical p.

The Gram matrix has proportional columns and determinant zero; it has no inverse. Selecting the single column basis u is sufficient to construct P. If a pseudoinverse is used, it must be derived correctly: A+=125[120240] yields the same minimum-norm coefficients and satisfies AA+=P. Unique physical projection and unique generator coordinates are different claims.

Problem 3. Determine the scale instead of assuming symmetry is enough

Original problem; independently derived solution.

For a nonzero real scalar a, consider M=a[1224]. For which a is M an orthogonal projection? Give its range and explain what fails at a=1/2.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Let B be the unscaled displayed matrix. Direct multiplication gives B2=5B. Since M is symmetric for every real a, the missing condition is idempotence. The equation M2=M becomes 5a2B=aB. Because B is nonzero and a is nonzero, this reduces to 5 a=1, so a=1/5. The excluded a=0 would give the zero-space projection, but it is outside the question's nonzero premise.

At a=1/5, M is uuT/(uTu) for u=(1,2), so its range is the line spanned by u and its kernel is the perpendicular line spanned by (−2,1). It fixes u and kills that normal. Those two actions give a direct decomposition certificate as well as the matrix identity test.

At a=1/2, the matrix remains symmetric and has the same range, but it multiplies u by 5/2 instead of fixing it. Applying it twice scales that component by 25/4, which differs from the first application. Thus range information and symmetry do not establish that the map is a projection. The error is an incorrect normalization, not a changed geometric line. A rank-one outer product requires division by the generator's squared length; rescaling the generator without preserving that normalization changes the operator.

Problem 4. Weighted perpendicularity can look nonsymmetric

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Use the weighted inner product ⟨x,y⟩W=xTWy with W=diag(1,4). Project b=(2,−1) onto the line spanned by u=(1,1). Find the matrix and verify a weighted energy split. Is the projector symmetric in ordinary coordinates?

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The projection coefficient is (uTWb)/(uTWu). Its numerator is 2−4=−2 and its denominator is 1+4=5. Therefore p=(−2/5,−2/5) and r=(12/5,−3/5). The matrix is

PW=u(uTWu)-1uTW=15[1414].

It is not ordinarily symmetric because its off-diagonal entries differ. Nevertheless it is idempotent and satisfies the correct weighted self-adjoint relation PWTW=WPW. Weighted perpendicularity is verified by uTWr=12/5+4(-3/5)=0. Ordinary u transpose r is 9/5 rather than zero, so applying the ordinary Euclidean perpendicularity test would reject a valid weighted projection.

The original weighted squared norm is 22+4(-1)2=8. The projected energy is 5(2/5)2=4/5, and the residual energy is (12/5)2+4(3/5)2=36/5. Their sum is eight. This Pythagorean identity uses the same positive-definite W as the projection. Mixing an ordinary norm on one side with weighted energies on the other would compare different metrics. A nonsymmetric matrix can thus be an orthogonal projector in a declared weighted geometry while failing ordinary Euclidean orthogonality.

Finite geometry for this problem

Problem 5. An affine hyperplane is not a linear subspace

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Find the closest point to b=(3,1,0) on the affine plane x+2y-z=3, and its squared distance. State the affine projection map and explain why it is not linear.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The normal is n=(1,2,−1), with squared length six. Its dot product with b is five, exceeding the required plane value by two. Subtract the normal correction:

p=b-nTb-3nTnn=(8/3,1/3,1/3)T.

The plane equation checks directly: 8/3+2/3−1/3=3. The residual b−p=(1/3,2/3,−1/3) is a multiple of n and therefore perpendicular to every direction lying in the plane. Its squared norm is (1+4+1)/9=2/3. The direction-space certificate establishes unique closest-point optimality: subtracting any other point in the same plane creates a direction perpendicular to this residual.

For general input x, the closest-point map is F(x)=(I-nnT/6)x+n/2. Its constant term is nonzero, so F(0)=n/2 rather than zero. Thus F is affine but not linear. It fixes every point on the plane and satisfies F(F(x))=F(x), yet those properties alone do not make it a linear projection matrix. Translating the plane to its parallel subspace, projecting the translated vector, and translating back provides another derivation. The distinction prevents replacing an affine constraint by a homogeneous one and returning the wrong closest point.

Problem 6. A commuting product and a nonprojecting sum

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Let P=diag(1,1,0) and Q=diag(0,1,1). Determine projectors onto the intersection and sum of their ranges. Is P+Q itself a projection?

Read the complete solution and independent checks

P selects the first two coordinate directions, and Q selects the last two. They commute because both are diagonal. Their common range is the second coordinate axis, and PQ=diag(0,1,0) is its projector. The sum of the ranges is the whole three-dimensional space, whose projector is P+Q-PQ=I. The subtraction removes the double count of the common coordinate.

The plain sum P+Q is diag(1,2,1). It sends e₂ to 2 e₂, so it does not fix a vector in its alleged range; squaring gives diag(1,4,1), which differs. It is symmetric and positive semidefinite but not idempotent. A trace value four is also incompatible with an ordinary orthogonal projector in dimension three.

More generally, for commuting orthogonal projectors, PQ is symmetric and idempotent because transposition reverses the product and commutation restores it, while (PQ)2=P2Q2=PQ. Its range lies in both ranges and it fixes their intersection. The complementary commuting product (I−P)(I−Q) projects onto the intersection of the complements. Taking its complement gives P+Q−PQ, the sum-space projector. Without commutation these algebraic simplifications are invalid. A formula verified on diagonal examples must still have its general hypothesis declared before use.

Problem 7. A fractional trace refutes an intersection shortcut

Original problem; independently derived solution.

In the plane, let P project onto the first coordinate axis and Q onto the line spanned by (1,1). Compute PQ, decide whether it is a projection, and compare its trace with the dimension of the intersection.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The matrices and product are

P=[1000],Q=12[1111],PQ=12[1100].

The reverse product is one half of the matrix with rows (1,0) and (1,0), so the two products differ. Squaring PQ gives one quarter of its unscaled displayed matrix, or one half of PQ. Thus PQ is not idempotent and is not an orthogonal projector. It is also nonsymmetric.

The two distinct lines intersect only at zero, so their intersection dimension is zero. But trace(PQ)=1/2. The equality between trace and rank applies to an idempotent matrix; it cannot be applied to an arbitrary product of idempotent matrices. Here the product's nonzero eigenvalue is 1/2 rather than one, reflecting attenuation caused by the angle between the lines.

As an additional exact check, ‖P-Q‖F2=1. The identity rank(P)+rank(Q)−2 trace(PQ) gives 1+1−1=1, agreeing with direct entrywise squares. This geometric trace identity does not turn the fractional trace into an integer intersection dimension. The counterexample pinpoints the missing commutation premise rather than rejecting every useful relationship between two projection matrices.

Finite geometry for this problem

Problem 8. Conjugation is a substantive operation

Original problem; independently derived solution.

In complex Euclidean space, project b=(1,1) onto the line generated by u=(1,i), using the convention conjugate-linear in the first argument. Find p and r and diagnose the ordinary-transpose formula.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The squared norm is u*u=1+(-i)i=2. The coefficient is u*b/2=(1-i)/2, so

P=12[1-ii1],p=12[1-i1+i],r=12[1+i1-i].

The projector is Hermitian: its off-diagonal entries are conjugates. The residual check is u*r=(1+i)/2-i(1-i)/2=0. Each projected coordinate has squared magnitude 1/2, so the projected squared norm is one; the residual also has squared norm one. Their sum equals the original squared norm two, confirming the complex Pythagorean split.

Using u transpose instead would produce uTu=1+i2=0 even though u is nonzero. That expression is not a positive-definite squared norm and cannot appear as the denominator of this Hermitian projection formula. The problem is not numerical roundoff; it is the wrong bilinear form. Other authors use a first-argument-linear convention, which changes the written coefficient orientation. Either convention can work if applied consistently, but a displayed conjugate must not be dropped during transcription or inferred solely from a real-valued example.

Problem 9. Diagonal data reveals fixed and killed coordinates

Original problem; independently derived solution.

An ordinary orthogonal projector has diagonal (1,1/2,1/2). Determine its possible matrices in three dimensions. Explain why diagonal (1,0,1/2) cannot be the diagonal of another such projector.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

For an orthogonal projector, Pjj=‖Pej‖2 and 1-Pjj=‖(I-P)ej‖2. A first diagonal entry one forces (I−P)e₁=0, hence Pe₁=e₁. Symmetry then fixes the first row and column as (1,0,0). The remaining symmetric block has the form [1/2tt1/2].

Its idempotence equation on a diagonal entry is 1/4+t²=1/2, giving t=±1/2. The off-diagonal equation is already t=t. Thus exactly two matrices fit: first coordinate fixed, with a rank-one projector onto either (0,1,1) or (0,1,−1) in the remaining coordinate plane. Both have total trace two and rank two.

By contrast, diagonal (1,0,1/2) would have trace 3/2. Over the declared real finite-dimensional model, every idempotent matrix has eigenvalues zero or one and is diagonalizable, so its trace is its integer rank. The fractional value rules out existence. Bounds placing every diagonal entry in [0,1] are necessary but not sufficient. A diagonal value zero also forces the corresponding row and column to vanish for an orthogonal projector, because the projected coordinate vector has zero norm. These structural constraints provide more information than a numerical trace check alone.

Problem 10. Idempotence does not control Euclidean expansion

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Let E=[1t00] with real t≠0. Determine its image, kernel and Euclidean operator norm. Is it an ordinary orthogonal projection despite E squared equaling E?

Read the complete solution and independent checks

E maps (x,y) to (x+ty,0). Its image is the first coordinate axis and its kernel is the line x+ty=0, generated by (−t,1). Direct multiplication verifies E²=E, so it is an algebraic projector onto its image along that kernel. The kernel is not perpendicular to the image when t≠0.

The output length is |x+ty|. For a unit input, Cauchy–Schwarz bounds this by 1+t2, and the input (1,t)/1+t2 attains that bound. Therefore ‖E‖2=1+t2>1. The matrix is nonsymmetric, and it expands some unit vectors. Both facts distinguish it from an ordinary orthogonal projection, which is contractive.

For example, E sends b=(0,1) to p=(t,0), with residual r=(−t,1). The residual dot e₁ is −t rather than zero, so the closest-point certificate fails; the actual orthogonal projection of b onto the image is zero. Eigenvalues zero and one, integer trace one, and idempotence establish an algebraic projection but do not establish orthogonality. The example explains why a spectral-radius bound of one is not an operator-norm bound of one for a nonnormal matrix. The geometry of the kernel and the declared inner product are essential.

Finite geometry for this problem

Problem 11. A perpendicular pair is not a complete certificate

Original problem; independently derived solution.

A candidate projection of b=(1,1,1)T onto S=span(e1,e2) is p=e1. It satisfies pT(b-p)=0. Is it the closest point? Give a necessary and sufficient certificate instead.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The proposed residual is r=(0,1,1)T. Its dot product with p=e1 is indeed zero, and the candidate belongs to the plane. But e2Tr=1, so the residual is not perpendicular to the entire plane. The candidate has squared error two. The point (1,1,0)T belongs to the plane and has squared error one, proving the proposed answer is wrong.

The complete certificate requires both p∈S and vT(b-p)=0 for every v∈S. It suffices to check every member of any spanning set. If those conditions hold, then for any z∈S, b-z=(b-p)+(p-z) has perpendicular components. Consequently its squared length is ‖b-p‖2+‖p-z‖2, minimized uniquely at z=p. A single vanishing scalar product cannot replace a whole-subspace condition when the subspace has more than one direction.

Problem 12. Project onto a kernel without finding its basis

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Find the Euclidean projection onto S={x:x1+2x2+2x3=0}, then project b=(3,0,0)T and calculate the distance.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The constraint normal is n=(1,2,2)T and nTn=9. The normal-line projection is nnT/9. Subtracting it from the identity gives

P=19(8-2-2-25-4-2-45).

Thus p=(8/3,-2/3,-2/3)T and r=(1/3,2/3,2/3)T=n/3. Substituting p into the constraint gives 8/3-4/3-4/3=0, so it is feasible. The residual is a normal multiple, providing the perpendicularity certificate. Its squared length is one, so the distance is one.

The matrix has trace two, consistent with one independent constraint in three dimensions. The normal-line projector has trace one. Confusing these complementary operators returns the residual instead of the closest point. The method avoids solving for two plane generators, but it relies on a nonzero normal: a zero constraint normal either imposes no homogeneous restriction or makes a nonzero affine right-hand side inconsistent.

Problem 13. Orthogonal but unnormalized generators

Berkeley Math 54 projection example, independently explained and checked.

Project b=(4,8,1)T onto the span of v1=(2,1,2)T and v2=(-2,2,1)T. Can their outer products simply be added?

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Their dot product is -4+2+2=0, and both squared lengths are nine. Their products with the target are eighteen and nine. Therefore the correct projection is p=2v1+v2=(2,4,5)T. The residual (2,4,-4)T has zero dot product with each generator, and its squared length is thirty-six.

The matrix is (v1v1T+v2v2T)/9. Adding the unscaled outer products produces 9P, which acts by nine on every vector in the plane; it is not idempotent. If normalized generators ui=vi/3 are used, the formula becomes u1u1T+u2u2T with no extra denominator.

The energy check is ‖b‖2=81, ‖p‖2=45, and ‖r‖2=36. This independently confirms the squared distance. The distinction between orthogonal and orthonormal is substantive: perpendicularity separates the coefficient equations, while unit normalization removes their denominators. This is an independently explained reconstruction of the numerical example in Berkeley's projection notes, pages three and four.

Problem 14. Recover a projector from its action

Original problem; independently derived solution.

An orthogonal projector on ℝ3 fixes u=(1,1,0)T and kills v=(1,-1,0)T. Does this determine it uniquely? List all possibilities.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Normalize these perpendicular vectors to q1=u/2 and q2=v/2, and complete them with q3=e3. Symmetry implies ⟨Pq3,q1⟩=⟨q3,Pq1⟩=0 and ⟨Pq3,q2⟩=⟨q3,Pq2⟩=0. Thus Pq3 is a scalar multiple λq3. Idempotence forces λ2=λ, giving zero or one.

The two possibilities in standard coordinates are

P0=12(110110000),P1=P0+e3e3T.

Their ranks are one and two. Both satisfy every given action. The unspecified perpendicular direction creates a genuine ambiguity; counting the two supplied vectors does not establish that all three directions have been characterized. If the problem additionally states rank one, only the first remains. Without orthogonality, a third input could map obliquely into the fixed line and produce still more idempotent maps.

Problem 15. A rank-one update when a new generator is added

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Suppose P projects onto S and a vector v is added to its generators. Derive the new projector and handle v∈S separately. Apply the result to S=span(e1) and v=(1,2,2)T.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Split v=Pv+w with w=(I-P)v. If w=0, the new vector was already in S, so the subspace and projector are unchanged. If w≠0, the enlarged space is the perpendicular direct sum of S and the line spanned by w. Consequently

Pnew=P+wwTwTw.

The cross-products vanish because Pw=0, so the sum is symmetric and idempotent. Its range is the enlarged subspace, and its rank increases by exactly one. This derives the update and explains its denominator rather than guessing an outer product of the original v.

In the example w=(0,2,2)T, giving Pnew=(10001/21/201/21/2). For b=(0,1,-1)T, both its projection and the update contribution are zero, so its squared distance remains two. Using vvT/(vTv) instead would double-count a component already present in S.

Problem 16. A nonorthogonal change of basis

Original problem; independently derived solution.

The physical projector is P=diag(1,0), but coordinates use B=(1101). Compute the coordinate projector and its correct metric. Explain its nonsymmetry.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The inverse basis matrix is B-1=(1-101). Direct multiplication gives E=B-1PB=(1100). The coordinate metric is G=BTB=(1112). We obtain E2=E and ETG=GE=(1111).

For the physical vector b=e2, its coordinates are z=(-1,1)T. The coordinate projection is Ez=0, corresponding to the correct physical closest point zero. Its coordinate residual equals z, whose squared G -length is one, agreeing with the physical squared distance.

Ordinary coordinate symmetry is absent because the chosen basis vectors are not perpendicular. Testing ET=E would use the wrong metric. In contrast, treating that same numerical matrix as a map in a separately declared ordinary Euclidean coordinate system would make it oblique. A basis change preserves the geometric map only when its metric is transformed as well.

Problem 17. Derive a Householder reflection

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Reflect b=(3,0)T across the line x+y=0. Find the reflection matrix, its determinant and the associated closest-point projection.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The normal is n=(1,1)T. Projection onto the reflecting line is P=I-nnT/2=12(1-1-11). Therefore H=2P-I=(0-1-10) and Hb=(0,-3)T. The projected point is Pb=(3/2,-3/2)T, the midpoint of b and its reflection.

The determinant of H is minus one, so this is a reflection rather than a rotation of the plane. Directly, HTH=I and H2=I; the input and reflected vectors have the same norm three. The direction (1,-1)T is fixed and the normal (1,1)T is negated.

The midpoint identity P=(I+H)/2 explains why averaging identity and reflection produces a closest-point map. The reflection itself is not idempotent: its second application returns the input. The projection is idempotent and discards the normal component. Confusing these two operations changes both the output and the spectrum.

Finite geometry for this problem

Problem 18. Quantify alternating projections

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Project alternately onto a line at sixty degrees and the horizontal axis, starting at e1. Count a full cycle as the sloping projection followed by the horizontal one. How many cycles make the norm at most 1/1000?

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Here c=1/2 and s=3/2. One cycle is M=PQ=(1/43/400). Since Me1=e1/4, induction gives Mje1=4-je1. The question asks for 4j≥1000. Four cycles give denominator 256, which is insufficient; five give 1024, which is sufficient. Thus exactly five cycles are needed.

The intermediate sloping point in cycle j is 4-(j-1)(1/4,3/4)T, and the next horizontal point is (4-j,0)T. These are actual finite vectors, not the intersection projector. The two lines intersect only at zero, which is reached as a limit for this input, not after any finite cycle.

If a simulation counts each individual projection as a step, it requires ten individual steps rather than five. Stating what one iteration means prevents a factor-of-two error. A nearly parallel pair would have a contraction factor close to one and require many more cycles.

Finite geometry for this problem

Problem 19. A commutator and a quantitative angle

Original problem; independently derived solution.

For the horizontal projector P and the projector Q onto (cosθ,sinθ)T, compute PQ-QP and its squared Frobenius norm. When do they commute?

Read the complete solution and independent checks

With c=cosθ and s=sinθ, multiplication gives

PQ-QP=(0cs-cs0),‖PQ-QP‖F2=2c2s2.

Thus the two maps commute exactly when cs=0. In the interval from zero to ninety degrees this means coincident lines or perpendicular lines. At forty-five degrees the squared norm is one half, the largest possible value for this family, since c2s2≤1/4.

The commutator is skew-symmetric, as transposition reverses its sign. It records an order effect: applying one projection before the other usually changes the result. It is not itself a projection merely because its factors are projections. A zero commutator is enough to construct the intersection projector by multiplication, but the numerical size of the commutator alone is not the intersection dimension or a count of violated constraints. The angle calculation makes the distinction explicit.

Problem 20. Equal ranks do not imply equal ranges

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Two rank-two orthogonal projectors in ℝ3 satisfy tr(PQ)=3/2. Find ‖P-Q‖F2 and the dimension of their intersection.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Expanding the squared Frobenius norm yields tr(P)+tr(Q)-2tr(PQ)=2+2-3=1. The dimension formula implies that two planes in three dimensions intersect in dimension at least one.

If their intersection had dimension two, their ranges would coincide. The orthogonal projector onto a fixed subspace is unique, so P=Q, giving tr(PQ)=tr(P)=2, contrary to the data. The intersection therefore has dimension exactly one. The trace value 3/2 itself is not a dimension.

To check realizability, let P project onto the plane spanned by e1,e2, and let Q project onto the plane spanned by e1,(e2+e3)/2. The common direction contributes one to the product trace and the remaining pair contributes one half. This constructs the stated overlap and confirms that the conditions are consistent, rather than merely extracting a formal number from them.

Problem 21. A projector polynomial without multiplication

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Let P be an idempotent matrix. Evaluate P7-3P2+2I and determine when aI+bP is invertible. Give its inverse when it exists.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Every positive power of P equals P by induction. The polynomial is therefore 2I-2P=2(I-P). More generally, on the range of P, the matrix aI+bP acts by a+b; on its kernel it acts by a. These subspaces form a direct sum even for oblique idempotents.

If both subspaces are nonzero, invertibility requires a≠0 and a+b≠0, and the inverse is

1a(I-P)+1a+bP.

Multiplying and using P(I-P)=0 verifies the formula. Endpoint ranks need care: if P=0, only a≠0 is required; if P=I, only a+b≠0 is required. A formula containing a denominator for a nonexistent component can impose an unnecessary restriction. This method uses idempotence rather than orthogonality, so it applies to oblique projectors too. Positivity and norm conclusions, by contrast, would require more information.

Problem 22. Rank from a shifted determinant

Original problem; independently derived solution.

An idempotent 5×5 real matrix satisfies det(I+2P)=27. Determine its rank and det(2I-P). Must the matrix be symmetric?

Read the complete solution and independent checks

A basis of the range followed by a basis of the kernel makes P similar to diag(Ik,0). Thus I+2P has k eigenvalues three and 5-k eigenvalues one. Its determinant is 3k=27, giving k=3.

The second shifted matrix acts by one on the range and by two on the kernel. Therefore det(2I-P)=1322=4. The trace of P is also three, but that fact does not imply symmetry. Similarity by an arbitrary invertible matrix preserves idempotence and these determinant values while generally destroying Euclidean symmetry.

For a concrete nonsymmetric construction, take a two-dimensional block (1100) and append diagonal entries 1,1,0. The resulting five-dimensional matrix has rank three and both required determinants, yet is not symmetric. Spectral calculations answer the rank question; they do not certify that the decomposition uses perpendicular subspaces.

Problem 23. All affine points from one constraint correction

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Minimize ‖x-b‖2 subject to Dx=d, where D=(110011), d=(1,2)T and b=(1,0,0)T.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The violation is Db-d=(0,-2)T. The row Gram matrix is (2112), whose inverse is 13(2-1-12). The multiplier is (2/3,-4/3)T, so the correction DTλ is (2/3,-2/3,-4/3)T. Therefore

p=(1/3,2/3,4/3)T,‖b-p‖2=8/3.

Both constraints check directly. Every feasible vector is p+t(-1,1,-1)T, and the residual (2/3,-2/3,-4/3)T is perpendicular to that direction. Thus the squared error for a general feasible vector is 8/3+3t2, proving unique minimality at t=0 without relying only on stationary equations.

The residual lies in the row space, while the feasible directions lie in the kernel. These are subspaces of the three-dimensional physical space. The multiplier has only two entries because it belongs to constraint space; adding it directly to b would be dimensionally invalid.

Problem 24. Dependent constraints: consistency comes first

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Compare closest-point problems with constraints x+y=1, 2x+2y=2 and with constraints x+y=1, 2x+2y=3. Use the target zero.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

In the first system the second equation is redundant. The feasible set is one line. Write y=1-x; the squared distance from zero is x2+(1-x)2=2(x-1/2)2+1/2. The unique closest point is (1/2,1/2)T with squared distance one half. The two-row Gram matrix is singular, but the geometry remains well-defined after retaining one independent row.

In the second system, doubling the first equation forces 2x+2y=2, contradicting the second equation. The feasible set is empty. There is no closest feasible point and no projection onto that empty set in the sense studied here.

An unconstrained least-squares fit to the inconsistent equations is a different optimization problem. With s=x+y, it minimizes (s-1)2+(2s-3)2, giving s=7/5. None of those minimizers satisfies either required pair exactly. A pseudoinverse cannot make incompatible constraints consistent; it can only solve a declared surrogate. Check the augmented rank before using an affine projection formula.

Problem 25. A weighted affine correction

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Minimize x2+4y2 subject to x+y=1. Compare the answer with ordinary Euclidean projection of zero onto the same line.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Substitute y=1-x. The objective is x2+4(1-x)2=5(x-4/5)2+4/5. Thus the unique weighted minimizer is (4/5,1/5)T with squared weighted distance 4/5. Ordinary Euclidean minimization instead gives (1/2,1/2)T.

The weighted correction formula explains the difference. With G=diag(1,4) and row constraint D=(1,1), the shortest correction from target b is

p=b-G-1DT(DG-1DT)-1(Db-1).

At zero, G-1DT=(1,1/4)T and DG-1DT=5/4, producing the same answer. The correction follows the metric normal G-1DT, not the ordinary normal DT.

The direction (1,-1)T lies in the line's direction space. Its weighted inner product with the minimizer is 4/5-4/5=0. This verifies the correct orthogonality certificate and explains conceptually why changing the cost weights changes the closest point.

Finite geometry for this problem

Problem 26. A semidefinite cost can lose uniqueness

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Minimize xTGx over x∈ℝ2 with G=diag(1,0). Then minimize the same cost subject to x1=1. Why does the positive-definite projection theorem not apply?

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The objective is simply x12. Unconstrained minimizers are all vectors (0,t)T, with arbitrary real t, and cost zero. Under x1=1, every feasible vector (1,t)T has cost one, so again there are infinitely many minimizers.

The matrix is positive semidefinite, not positive definite. The nonzero vector e2 has zero squared cost, violating the condition that zero length occurs only at the zero vector. Therefore xTGy is not an inner product on the full plane and its associated quantity is not a norm there.

The closest-point proof uses strict positivity of the extra squared difference to establish uniqueness. Here the extra term can vanish for different points separated in the unpenalized direction. A specific restricted feasible set might still have a unique minimizer, but uniqueness must then be proved from those restrictions. Substituting a singular weight into a formula derived for a positive-definite metric is not a valid general argument.

Problem 27. Classify an idempotent family

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Let Pa=(1a00) for real a. Find when it is Euclidean orthogonal, and find a positive-definite metric making it orthogonal for any fixed a.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Every member is idempotent. Euclidean symmetry requires a=0, which is also sufficient. For a general metric G=(ghhk), the self-adjoint condition PaTG=GPa requires h=ag. Positive definiteness then requires g>0 and k>a2g.

One valid choice is G=(1aaa2+1), whose determinant is one. Its quadratic form is (x+ay)2+y2, strictly positive for every nonzero vector. The range direction e1 and kernel direction (-a,1)T have zero G -product.

Thus an oblique Euclidean projector can be orthogonal for another declared metric. The numerical matrix alone does not specify what perpendicularity means. Conversely, inventing a new metric after a question explicitly states the ordinary dot product would change the problem. The distinction helps diagnose apparent disagreements between coordinate formulas without erasing their hypotheses.

Problem 28. Impossible diagonal and a sharp entry bound

Original problem; independently derived solution.

A real orthogonal projector has p11=1/4 and p22=3/4. Bound |p12|. Can equality occur in two dimensions?

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Cauchy–Schwarz for Pe1,Pe2 gives p122≤(1/4)(3/4)=3/16. Applying it to the complementary projector gives the same bound, so |p12|≤3/4.

In two dimensions the symmetric candidate is (1/4tt3/4). Idempotence on the first diagonal gives 1/16+t2=1/4, requiring t2=3/16. The other diagonal and off-diagonal equations then hold. Hence exactly the two signs t=±3/4 are possible, and each attains equality.

These are line projectors generated by unit vectors (1/2,±3/2)T. A candidate with the same diagonal and t=0 satisfies the entry bound but is not idempotent. Necessary inequalities help reject matrices; they do not replace the defining identities. In higher dimensions extra entries can contribute to row squared norms, so the two-dimensional equality conclusion cannot be inferred from these two diagonal entries alone.

Problem 29. Orthogonal decomposition of an observation vector

MIT 18.06 SC Session 2.3 exercise reconstruction; independently derived explanation. See exact exercise numbers in the question.

Reconstruct MIT Session 2.3 exercise 16.1: fit the observations (7,7,21)T at times (-1,1,2) with C+Dt. Derive the coefficients rather than quoting the answer.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The design columns are the all-ones vector and the time vector. Their Gram matrix is (3226), and their products with the observation vector give (35,42)T. The normal equations are 3C+2D=35 and 2C+6D=42. Eliminate C: multiplying the first equation by two and the second by three gives 6C+4D=70 and 6C+18D=126. Thus 14D=56, so D=4 and C=9.

The fitted observation vector is (5,13,17)T, lying in the two-dimensional column space in ℝ3. The coefficient vector (9,4)T instead lives in ℝ2. They describe different objects. Since the two columns are independent, their Gram matrix has positive determinant fourteen and this coefficient solution is unique. The calculation is a projection in observation space, not an orthogonal-distance line fit in the time-height plot.

Problem 30. Explain why projecting the error gives zero

MIT 18.06 SC Session 2.3 exercise reconstruction; independently derived explanation. See exact exercise numbers in the question.

Continue the preceding MIT exercise family 16.2–16.4. Find the residual, project that residual, and project the fitted vector again. Explain all three operations geometrically.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Subtracting fitted from observed values gives r=(2,-6,4)T. Its products with the two design columns are 2-6+4=0 and -2-6+8=0. Therefore it lies in the left nullspace and its orthogonal projection onto the column space is zero. Its squared norm is 4+36+16=56.

The fitted vector p=(5,13,17)T already belongs to that column space, so Pp=p. Thus the operator kills the error and fixes the fit: Pr=0 and Pp=p. For a general input b=p+r, linearity then gives Pb=p.

If the residual is used as a new response vector with the same design columns, the unique fitted coefficients are zero. If the fitted response is used instead, its coefficients remain (9,4)T and its residual becomes zero. These statements depend on keeping the same design space; changing the time points or columns changes the projector. The operations demonstrate complementary subspaces and idempotence rather than requiring another matrix inverse.

Problem 31. Locate each vector in its correct ambient space

MIT 18.06 SC Session 2.3 exercise reconstruction; independently derived explanation. See exact exercise numbers in the question.

Revisit the four-subspace issue in MIT exercise 16.5. For A∈ℝm×n, where do the fitted vector, residual and least-squares coefficients belong? What changes if the columns are dependent?

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The physical fit p belongs to Col(A)⊆ℝm. The residual belongs to Ker(AT)⊆ℝm. Any coefficient minimizer c belongs to ℝn and satisfies Ac=p. If the columns are independent, the row space of A is all of ℝn, so that unique coefficient vector lies in it automatically.

With dependent columns, every minimizer has the form c0+z, where z∈Ker(A). The unique minimum-norm minimizer is the one in Col(AT)=Ker(A)⊥. Other minimizers need not lie in the row space. For example, if A=(1,1) and the target is one, (1,0)T is a minimizer but is not on the row-space line spanned by (1,1)T; the minimum-norm choice is (1/2,1/2)T.

Thus the source's full-column-rank example cannot be generalized to every minimizer of a deficient system. This is a hypothesis check, not a disagreement with its stated example.

Problem 32. Symmetric times remove one coupling term

MIT 18.06 SC Session 2.3 exercise reconstruction; independently derived explanation. See exact exercise numbers in the question.

Reconstruct MIT exercise 16.6: fit values (4,2,-1,0,0)T at times (-2,-1,0,1,2) with an intercept and slope. Compute the fit and squared residual norm.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The time sum is zero and the sum of squared times is ten. Thus the Gram matrix is diag(5,10). The observation sum is five, and the time-weighted sum is -8-2=-10. Therefore the coefficient equations give C=1 and D=-1.

The fitted values are (3,2,1,0,-1)T, and the residual is (1,0,-2,0,1)T. Its sum and time-weighted sum are zero, as required by perpendicularity to both design columns. The squared error is 1+4+1=6. The input squared norm is twenty-one and the fitted squared norm is fifteen, giving the energy check 21=15+6.

Centering time values makes the constant and time columns perpendicular; it does not necessarily make either a unit vector. Their squared lengths remain five and ten, explaining the two denominators. Symmetry of the times simplifies this example, but orthogonality follows from zero sum even for nonsymmetric time sets. The distinction separates a sufficient convenient pattern from the exact algebraic condition.

Problem 33. QR from an explicit orthonormal pair

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Let q1=(1,1,0)T/2, q2=(1,-1,2)T/6, and Q=[q1q2]. Project b=e3 and find the complementary rank-one projector.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The vectors have unit norm and dot product zero. The coordinate measurements are QTb=(0,2/6)T. Reconstruction gives p=(1/3,-1/3,2/3)T. The residual is r=(-1/3,1/3,1/3)T, whose squared norm is one third.

A perpendicular unit vector is q3=(-1,1,1)T/3. Hence I-QQT=q3q3T, while QQT=I-q3q3T. This provides a second calculation of the same residual. The fitted squared norm is two thirds, summing with the residual energy to the unit input energy.

Although QTQ=I2, the product QQT is a three-dimensional rank-two projector and cannot equal I3. Its nullspace contains the nonzero vector q3. Rectangular orthonormality is one-sided; substituting the wrong identity would make the computed residual vanish and falsely claim that every three-dimensional vector lies in a two-dimensional plane.

Problem 34. Projection operators in a polynomial space

Original problem; independently derived solution.

In real polynomials of degree at most two, use ⟨f,g⟩=∫-11f(t)g(t)dt. Project f(t)=t2 onto the span of 1,t. Find the squared error.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The generators are perpendicular because ∫-11tdt=0. Their squared norms are two and 2/3. The target products are ∫-11t2dt=2/3 and ∫-11t3dt=0. Thus its projection is the constant polynomial p(t)=1/3.

The residual t2-1/3 has zero product with both generators. Its squared norm is

∫-11(t2-1/3)2dt=2/5-4/9+2/9=8/45.

The coefficient vector of f in the monomial basis is (0,0,1)T. Merely discarding the quadratic coordinate would give zero, which is wrong: the monomial basis is not orthonormal in this integral metric. Indeed the constant and quadratic monomials have nonzero product 2/3. Projection acts on functions with their declared inner product, not on an arbitrary coefficient list with an assumed Euclidean metric. The same finite-dimensional theorem applies once the correct Gram matrix is used.

Problem 35. Weighted complex projection

Original problem; independently derived solution.

In ℂ2, use G=diag(2,1) and project b=(1,1)T onto the complex line generated by u=(1,i)T.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The correct product is u*Gb=2-i, and u*Gu=3. Therefore the coefficient is (2-i)/3 and

p=13(2-i1+2i),r=13(1+i2-2i).

The matrix is PG=13(2-i2i1). It is generally not Hermitian under the ordinary complex dot product, but satisfies PG*G=GPG and is idempotent. The weighted residual certificate is u*Gr=2(1+i)/3-i(2-2i)/3=0.

The projected energy is |2-i|2/3=5/3, while the input energy is three. The residual energy is therefore 4/3; direct magnitude squares give the same value. Both conjugation and the metric are essential. Replacing G by the identity solves a different closest-point problem, while replacing the conjugate transpose by an ordinary transpose destroys positive definiteness.

Problem 36. Recover a subspace from a distance oracle

Original problem; independently derived solution.

An unknown orthogonal projector P on ℝ3 has squared residual distances zero for e1 and e2, and one for e3. Determine P. Would knowledge of the three diagonal distances always determine a projector?

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Zero distance for e1 implies (I-P)e1=0, hence Pe1=e1. The same reasoning fixes e2. Distance one for the unit vector e3 implies its projected energy is zero by Pythagoras, so Pe3=0. The action on this basis determines P=diag(1,1,0).

The endpoint distance values are decisive because a nonnegative squared norm can vanish only at zero. Intermediate values do not usually identify the directions. In the plane, the two different line projectors 12(1111) and 12(1-1-11) give squared residual distance one half for both coordinate unit vectors.

Thus diagonal observations determine how much coordinate energy is retained, but can conceal sign and orientation information. A reconstruction problem should distinguish this special endpoint case from a general uniqueness claim. Additional mixed-vector distance measurements can recover off-diagonal entries by polarization.

Problem 37. Recover an off-diagonal entry by polarization

Original problem; independently derived solution.

For an unknown real orthogonal projector, suppose the squared residual distances for e1,e2,e1+e2 are 1/2,1/2,0. Determine p11,p22,p12 and interpret the result in two dimensions.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The squared residual distance for x is xT(I-P)x. Applying it to the two unit vectors gives 1-p11=1/2 and 1-p22=1/2. Expanding for their sum gives 2-p11-p22-2p12=0, so p12=1/2.

In two dimensions this fixes P=12(1111), the projector onto the line spanned by (1,1)T. The zero residual distance for their sum says precisely that this direction belongs to the range.

The mixed measurement contains a cross term that separate coordinate measurements cannot reveal. The sign is easy to reverse if one uses projected energy instead of residual energy without changing the expansion. Checking the known range direction provides an immediate independent sign check. In a larger ambient dimension these entries specify only a principal block; other directions may still require measurements, although the fixed mixed vector imposes additional constraints.

Problem 38. A quadratic minimum with a projector penalty

Original problem; independently derived solution.

For an orthogonal projector P and real λ>0, minimize F(x)=‖x-b‖2+λ‖Px‖2. Give the minimum value.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Decompose b=bS+bN and x=xS+xN using the range and perpendicular kernel of P. Perpendicularity separates the objective into ‖xN-bN‖2+‖xS-bS‖2+λ‖xS‖2. Completing the square in the range component gives the unique minimizer

x*=(I-P)b+11+λPb.

The minimum is λ‖Pb‖2/(1+λ). The kernel component is left unchanged because the penalty does not act there; the range component is shrunk rather than removed entirely.

For P=diag(1,0), b=(3,4)T and λ=2, the answer is (1,4)T and the minimum is six. At finite positive penalty this map is generally not a projector: its range eigenvalue is 1/(1+λ), strictly between zero and one. As the penalty tends to infinity, it approaches the complementary projection. A shrinkage operator and an idempotent projection have different spectra and repeated-application behavior.

Problem 39. Closest-point projection can fail outside a subspace

Original problem; independently derived solution.

A proposed theorem claims every nonempty set has one unique closest point to every target. Refute it with a finite set, and explain the missing structure in the linear projection theorem.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Take the set C={(-1,0)T,(1,0)T} and target zero. Both candidates have squared distance one, so the minimizer exists but is not unique. There is no single-valued closest-point map without an arbitrary selection rule.

In the linear subspace theorem, differences of feasible points remain in the subspace. This lets the perpendicular residual split the squared error by Pythagoras, with a strictly positive extra term for every different point. The two-point set lacks the required feasible directions, and it is not convex.

The example does not say that only subspaces have unique closest points: nonempty closed convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space do too, by a broader theorem. Their projection maps, however, need not be linear. For instance projection onto the nonnegative real half-line sends a scalar to its maximum with zero. The present chapter's matrix identities characterize linear orthogonal projections, not every nearest-point operation on every possible set.

Problem 40. A tempting but false complement formula

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Let P,Q be orthogonal projectors. Is I-PQ always an orthogonal projection? Is P+Q-PQ always the projector onto the sum of their ranges?

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Use the horizontal projector and the forty-five-degree line projector from Problem 7. Their product is M=12(1100) and satisfies M2=M/2, not M. The complement I-M would be idempotent only if M2=M, as expanding (I-M)2=I-M shows. It therefore fails.

The proposed sum expression equals (101/21/2). It is nonsymmetric and does not equal the identity, even though the two nonparallel lines span the whole plane. Its square also differs from itself.

If P and Q commute, both formulas become valid orthogonal projectors: the first onto the complement of the intersection, the second onto the sum. Expanding a product of complements in a specified order is always algebraically valid, but concluding that the product is itself a projector requires the commutation hypothesis. Set identities alone do not license replacing intersection by arbitrary matrix multiplication.

Problem 41. A universal energy identity forces orthogonality

Original problem; independently derived solution.

A real square matrix E satisfies E2=E and ‖Ex‖2+‖(I-E)x‖2=‖x‖2 for every real vector x. Prove that E is an orthogonal projector. Would one tested input suffice?

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Expanding the identity gives xT(2ETE-E-ET)x=0 for every x. The matrix in parentheses is symmetric, so polarization or evaluating on coordinate sums shows that it is zero. Hence 2ETE=E+ET.

Alternatively, decompose arbitrary x=u+v with u in the range and v in the kernel of the idempotent. The proposed identity becomes ‖u‖2+‖v‖2=‖u+v‖2, forcing uTv=0 for every such pair. Thus the range and kernel are perpendicular, identifying E as the orthogonal projector.

One tested input is insufficient. The oblique projector (1100) satisfies the energy identity for input e1, since it fixes that vector. It fails for input e2: the projected and residual squared lengths are one and two, summing to three instead of one. Universal quantifiers distinguish operator identities from accidental equality on a sample.

Problem 42. Determine containment from one scalar

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Orthogonal projectors P,Q satisfy tr(PQ)=rank(P). Prove that the range of P is contained in the range of Q. Is this valid for arbitrary idempotents?

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Choose an orthonormal basis u1,…,ur of the range of P. The trace is ∑iuiTQui=∑i‖Qui‖2. Each summand is at most one by contraction. Since the sum equals r, every summand equals one. The perpendicular energy split then forces (I-Q)ui=0 for each basis vector, establishing containment.

The claim fails for general oblique idempotents. Take P=(1000) and Q=(1010). Both are idempotent, and the product has trace one, equal to the rank of P. But their ranges are different lines, generated by (1,0)T and (1,1)T.

The proof's crucial bounded summands came from orthogonal contraction. Integer eigenvalues of the individual idempotents do not recover that positivity argument for arbitrary products. Trace equalities must be interpreted with their structural hypotheses.

Problem 43. The difference of nested projectors

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Let S⊆U with dimensions two and four in ℝ6, and let P,Q be their orthogonal projectors. Describe Q-P, its rank, trace and kernel. Describe P-Q too.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Containment gives QP=PQ=P. Thus (Q-P)2=Q-2P+P=Q-P, and symmetry is immediate. Its range is U∩S⊥, which has dimension 4-2=2. It therefore has rank and trace two. Its kernel is the perpendicular direct sum S+U⊥, of dimension 2+(6-4)=4.

One can verify this action directly: vectors in S are fixed by both and cancel; vectors in U∩S⊥ are fixed only by Q; vectors in U⊥ are killed by both. These three perpendicular pieces exhaust the space.

The reverse difference P-Q acts by minus one on the two-dimensional middle piece and zero elsewhere. Its square is Q-P, so it is not idempotent here. Its trace is minus two and rank two. A difference formula needs both containment and the correct sign; symmetry alone does not determine which difference is a projection.

Problem 44. Rank changes invalidate a limiting shortcut

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Let Aε=(110ε). Find the projector onto its columns and the coefficients fitting b=e2 for nonzero ε. Compare with ε=0.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

For nonzero ε, the determinant is ε, so the columns span the whole plane. The orthogonal projector is I, independent of the parameter. Solving Aεc=e2 gives εc2=1 and c1+c2=0, hence c=(-1/ε,1/ε)T. Coefficients diverge as the parameter tends to zero, although the fitted vector remains exactly e2.

At zero the columns coincide and span the horizontal line. Its projector is diag(1,0), and the projected target is zero, with squared residual distance one. Thus the limit of the projectors at nonzero parameters is not the projector of the limiting matrix.

The discontinuity occurs at a rank change. It does not contradict uniqueness for any fixed subspace or imply that every small perturbation produces a discontinuity at fixed rank. A numerical procedure declaring a tiny parameter to be zero changes the modeled subspace and needs an explicit rank policy.

Problem 45. Best approximation from orthogonal measurements

Original problem; independently derived solution.

A vector b has squared norm twenty-five. Its inner products with three orthonormal vectors are 2,-3,1. Find the closest vector in their span and the distance. Could the three reported measurements instead be 4,3,2?
