Read the complete solution and independent checks

Orthogonality decouples the measurements, so the closest vector is p=2q1-3q2+q3. Its squared norm is 4+9+1=14. Pythagoras gives residual squared norm 25-14=11, so the distance is 11. The formula identifies a physical vector in the declared basis even if its ambient coordinates are not supplied.

The alternate measurements would have squared sum 16+9+4=29, exceeding the target's squared norm twenty-five. They are impossible for three orthonormal measurement vectors, by the same perpendicular energy identity or Bessel's inequality. The contradiction could indicate wrong data, nonunit vectors, or nonorthogonal directions, but the question's stated assumptions rule all three measurements out together.

An incomplete orthonormal set need not recover all the input energy; the remaining eleven can lie in its perpendicular complement. Equality of measured and total energy would certify membership in the measured span. These are exact feasibility conclusions, not statistical estimates.

Problem 46. Distance from a rank-one projector to another

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Let P=uuT and Q=vvT for real unit vectors. Derive their squared Frobenius distance and find its possible range. Does replacing v by -v change it?

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The product is PQ=u(uTv)vT, whose trace is (uTv)2. Both ranks are one, so

‖P-Q‖F2=2(1-(uTv)2).

Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the squared dot product between zero and one. The squared distance lies between zero and two. Zero occurs exactly when the two lines coincide, including the case v=-u. Two occurs for perpendicular lines. Intermediate angles produce intermediate values.

Replacing v by its negative leaves the outer product unchanged, and the squared dot product also remains unchanged. The distance compares unoriented subspaces, not signed unit-vector representatives. In contrast, the ordinary vector distance ‖u-v‖ distinguishes v=u from v=-u. The formula uses a matrix Frobenius norm, so interpreting its maximum as the Euclidean distance between the original endpoints would mix two spaces and two geometric objects.

Problem 47. Projection onto a diagonal line in arbitrary dimension

Original problem; independently derived solution.

Project b=(1,2,…,m)T onto the all-ones line in ℝm, for positive integer m. Find the squared distance and handle m=1.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

With generator u=(1,…,1)T, the denominator uTu=m. The coefficient is the coordinate mean (m+1)/2. Thus every projected coordinate equals that mean and P=uuT/m.

Using the sum and sum-of-squares formulas, the residual energy is

∑j=1m(j-m+12)2=m(m2-1)12.

To derive it, expand the square into ∑j2-(m+1)∑j+m(m+1)2/4, then substitute ∑j=m(m+1)/2 and ∑j2=m(m+1)(2m+1)/6. A common denominator twelve yields the stated expression. The residual sum is zero, proving perpendicularity to the all-ones direction.

At m=1, the line is the full space, the projector is the identity, and the formula gives zero error. Dividing by m is valid because m is positive; a zero-dimensional empty-data version is not included. This example connects centering to a projection while keeping the exact finite-dimensional assumptions explicit.

Problem 48. Centering is a complementary projection

Original problem; independently derived solution.

For m≥2, let J=uuT/m with u the all-ones vector. Show that C=I-J centers data, find its rank, and prove that centering twice has no further effect.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

Each coordinate of Jb is the mean b¯=∑ibi/m, so Cb has coordinates bi-b¯. Their sum is zero. The matrix J is symmetric and satisfies J2=J because uTu=m. Hence C is symmetric and C2=I-2J+J2=C.

The centered space is u⊥, of dimension m-1, so C has rank and trace m-1. Its kernel is the all-ones line. Centering a vector already of zero sum leaves it unchanged, explaining idempotence operationally.

The energy identity becomes ∑ibi2=mb¯2+∑i(bi-b¯)2. The first term is the squared norm of the mean vector, not merely the square of the scalar mean. Omitting the factor m confuses those objects. This deterministic identity does not by itself justify any statistical unbiasedness correction; such a claim requires a sampling model and belongs to the probability/statistics chapters.

Problem 49. A coordinate formula can be algebraically idempotent but wrong

Original problem; independently derived solution.

For A=(101101), a solution replaces its pivot columns by those of its reduced row-echelon form and constructs a projector from them. Demonstrate the error with a target.

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The original columns are independent. The reduced form has columns e1,e2 in the ambient three-space, so the incorrect construction gives Pwrong=diag(1,1,0). That is a valid projector, but onto a different plane. Row operations preserve linear relations among columns, not the physical column space in the original coordinates.

The original plane has normal n=(1,-1,1)T, so its correct projector is I-nnT/3. For target b=e3, this gives p=(-1/3,1/3,2/3)T, with squared residual distance one third. The incorrect projector gives zero and squared distance one.

Membership checks expose the error: the original plane satisfies x1-x2+x3=0, but the wrongly selected basis direction e1 violates that equation. Checking symmetry and idempotence alone certifies a closest-point map onto its own range, not that its range matches the subspace asked about. Use original pivot columns after reduction identifies their indices.

Problem 50. Synthesize weighted projection, coordinates and uniqueness

Original problem; independently derived solution.

In ℝ2 with G=(2112), project b=(2,0)T onto the line generated by u=(1,-1)T. Find the matrix, point, residual and weighted energies. Why is the answer unique?

Read the complete solution and independent checks

The metric has positive leading principal minors two and three, so it is positive definite. Here Gu=u, uTGu=2, and uTGb=2. Therefore the coefficient is one and p=(1,-1)T, with r=(1,1)T.

The weighted projector is PG=u(uTGu)-1uTG=12(1-1-11). It happens to be ordinarily symmetric in this example because the chosen line and its ordinary perpendicular complement are metric eigendirections. Ordinary symmetry is not generally guaranteed for a weighted projector.

The input energy is eight, the projected energy two, and the residual energy six. Their weighted cross term is zero because uTGr=0. For every competing point tu on the line, the error energy is six plus 2(1-t)2, proving unique minimality at one. The existence of a matrix formula is not the uniqueness proof; strict positivity of the metric on every nonzero feasible direction is. This closes the chapter by combining a concrete calculation with the underlying certificate.

Authentic examination revisits and a matrix-space extension

These two archive questions were also used in the orthogonality chapter. They are explicit revisits, not newly discovered distinct examination items. The PhD item tests this chapter directly; the MSc item is followed by an additional projection derivation. Answers are independently derived, not an official key.

MSc CS 1405 · Question 41

Original booklet · PDF page 9

Let W be the vector space of real symmetric 4×4 matrices whose trace is zero. What is dimW?

  1. 10
  2. 9
  3. 8
  4. 7
Read the independently derived complete answer

Correct option: 2.

A symmetric four-by-four matrix is determined by four diagonal entries and six entries strictly above the diagonal. Thus the full symmetric space has dimension ten. Trace is a nonzero linear functional on this space: for example, its value on E11 is one. Its kernel therefore has dimension 10-1=9, giving option 2. To see the independence directly, use the six matrices Eij+Eji for i<j and the three matrices E11-E44,E22-E44,E33-E44. Their distinct off-diagonal and first three diagonal coordinates prove independence, and the trace condition forces the remaining diagonal coordinate. Option 1 omits the independent trace constraint. Options 3 and 4 incorrectly subtract further constraints; symmetry has already been included in the count of ten. Under the Frobenius product, trace is the product with I. The trace-zero subspace is its perpendicular complement inside the ten-dimensional symmetric space. Thus exactly one nonzero normal direction is removed. The projector is X-tr(X)I/4, which is distinct from entrywise removal of the whole diagonal.

For a real symmetric matrix X, the closest trace-zero symmetric matrix under the Frobenius product is X-tr(X)I/4. It is feasible because its trace is zero. The residual is the scalar matrix tr(X)I/4, perpendicular to every trace-zero symmetric matrix since its Frobenius product with Y is tr(X)tr(Y)/4=0. This proves optimality and uniqueness by the same squared-distance theorem. For X=diag(1,2,3,4), subtract 5I/2, giving diagonal (-3/2,-1/2,1/2,3/2). The squared residual norm is 4(5/2)2=25. Removing the entire diagonal instead discards additional feasible trace-zero directions and is not the closest point in general.

PhD CS 1404 · Question 31

Original booklet · PDF page 8

Let {u1,…,un} be an orthonormal basis of a subspace U⊆ℝm, with n≤m. Define Px=∑k=1n⟨x,uk⟩uk. Which statement is false?

  1. P is idempotent.

  2. If x∈U, then Px∈U.

  3. For every x∈ℝm, |x|2≤|Px|2.

  4. P is a linear operator from ℝm to U.

Read the independently derived complete answer

Correct option: 3.

Every image is a linear combination of the basis vectors, so it lies in U. Linearity follows from linearity of the real inner product in x. If x=∑akuk belongs to U, orthonormality gives ⟨x,uk⟩=ak, hence Px=x; in particular, P(Px)=Px. Moreover r=x-Px is orthogonal to every uk because ⟨r,uj⟩=⟨x,uj⟩-⟨x,uj⟩=0. The orthogonal decomposition gives |x|22=|Px|22+|r|22, so the universally valid inequality is |Px|2≤|x|2. The inequality in option 3 is not valid for arbitrary permitted subspaces: take U=span{(1,0)} and x=(0,1). Then Px=0 while |x|2=1. If U=ℝm, both norms agree; that special case does not establish option 3 as a general statement. The animation uses a two-dimensional orthogonal decomposition with labelled actual lengths, rather than pretending to draw arbitrary m dimensions.

Summary: the complete reasoning chain

A projection problem starts with a target, a feasible space and a metric. For a finite-dimensional subspace with a positive-definite inner product, the target has a unique decomposition into a feasible component and a component perpendicular to every feasible direction. The first component is the unique closest point. This single certificate derives the matrix formula, its invariance under a basis change, symmetry in an orthonormal coordinate system, idempotence, contraction and the perpendicular energy identity.

Generator coordinates are auxiliary. Repeating columns changes the coefficient descriptions without changing the subspace or its physical closest point. Independent columns permit a Gram inverse; dependent columns require a basis selection or a correctly defined pseudoinverse. Affine constraints require feasibility and translation. Weighted and complex formulas require the corresponding metric and adjoint. Products, sums and differences require additional geometric hypotheses. A successful calculation should end by verifying the geometric certificate in the same ambient space and metric that defined the question.

Examination decisions and traps, with their reasons

Identify the object before selecting a formula

Decision 1

State the ambient space. If generators form an m×n matrix, the projected vector has m entries and a generator coefficient vector has n. A candidate formula with the wrong output dimension is invalid before any arithmetic is attempted.

Decision 2

State the metric. Ordinary Euclidean geometry uses transpose; complex Euclidean geometry uses conjugate transpose; a declared positive-definite metric inserts its matrix in the inner products. A diagram of ordinary coordinate angles cannot alone certify weighted perpendicularity.

Decision 3

Distinguish a subspace from an affine space. A linear subspace contains zero. An affine space may not. Its closest-point map generally has a nonzero constant term and is therefore affine rather than linear.

Decision 4

Test feasibility of multiple affine constraints. A dependent consistent system still has a closest point. An inconsistent system defines an empty feasible set. A least-squares surrogate for incompatible equations is a different problem and must be named as such.

Decision 5

Separate generators from a basis. A spanning list may contain zeros or dependencies. Orthogonal projection remains unique, but the full generator Gram matrix may have no inverse. Select independent original columns before using the inverse formula.

Decision 6

Use row reduction only to identify column indices. Original pivot columns span the physical column space. Pivot columns copied from the reduced matrix usually span a transformed space. A perfectly symmetric idempotent matrix may still project onto that wrong space.

Construct and verify a closest point

Decision 7

Use both parts of the certificate. A candidate p must belong to the desired subspace and b-p must be perpendicular to every generating direction. Neither membership alone nor perpendicularity to p alone is sufficient.

Decision 8

Prove uniqueness with the squared-distance split. For every feasible s, ‖b-s‖2=‖b-p‖2+‖p-s‖2. The final term is strictly positive when s≠p, which proves more than stationarity.

Decision 9

Use the line formula only with a nonzero generator. For a line generated by u, P=uuT/(uTu). A zero generator describes the zero subspace, whose projector is zero; division by its squared length is undefined.

Decision 10

Keep normalization with orthogonal generators. The coefficient of a nonunit orthogonal generator is (uiTb)/(uiTui). The denominators disappear only for an orthonormal list. Omitting them changes the operator's eigenvalues.

Decision 11

Justify Gram invertibility. For independent columns, zTCTCz=‖Cz‖2>0 for nonzero z. The proof fails when columns are dependent, regardless of whether the matrix dimensions happen to be square.

Decision 12

Check basis invariance. Replacing a basis C by CR with invertible R must leave P unchanged. Coefficients transform by R-1. Physical projection is an operator on vectors, not a preferred coordinate convention.

Decision 13

Use a normal when it is simpler. A hyperplane through zero with normal n has projector I-nnT/(nTn). The subtracted outer product projects onto the perpendicular normal line; it is not the hyperplane projector itself.

Decision 14

Treat the sign of the residual consistently. This chapter uses r=b-p. Some courses use p-b. Their orthogonality and squared-distance statements agree, but a displayed residual vector must have the chosen sign.

Decision 15

Do not infer membership from a low residual alone. Exact mathematics requires the stated equation. In approximate numerical work a tolerance and a norm must be declared. Rounding an entry to zero can change a rank or a feasibility decision.

Recognize the operator algebraically

Decision 16

Require symmetry and idempotence in ordinary real coordinates. Together they characterize Euclidean orthogonal projection. Symmetry alone allows scaling, while idempotence alone allows oblique range-kernel decompositions.

Decision 17

Interpret an idempotent without extra geometry. Every idempotent fixes its range, kills its kernel and is diagonalizable into zero and one blocks. Its trace equals its rank even if its range and kernel are not perpendicular.

Decision 18

Do not confuse orthogonal projections with orthogonal matrices. A proper projection loses information and is singular. An orthogonal matrix preserves all norms and is invertible. Among orthogonal projectors only the identity is an orthogonal matrix on the whole ambient space.

Decision 19

Use contraction with its universal quantifier. An idempotent contracting every vector is orthogonal. Observing no expansion for one vector is inadequate; an oblique map can fix one direction while expanding another.

Decision 20

Handle zero and full ranks explicitly. The zero projector has operator norm zero; every nonzero orthogonal projector has operator norm one. Full rank forces an idempotent to be the identity. The determinant of a proper projector is zero.

Decision 21

Reduce positive powers before multiplying large matrices. Idempotence gives Pj=P for positive integers. Therefore any polynomial in P is determined by its values at zero and one. This works for oblique idempotents as well.

Decision 22

Check which eigenspaces actually exist before imposing denominators. The inverse formula for aI+bP needs a≠0 on a nonzero kernel and a+b≠0 on a nonzero range. Endpoint ranks may remove one of those requirements.

Decision 23

Use positivity only for the orthogonal case. An orthogonal projector satisfies xTPx=‖Px‖2 and 0≤xTPx≤xTx. A general oblique idempotent can fail these equalities and inequalities.

Decision 24

Use the Frobenius norm with the correct object. An orthogonal projector has squared Frobenius norm equal to its rank. This is a sum over all matrix entries, whereas the operator norm is a maximum over unit input vectors.

Read coordinate and metric information

Decision 25

Interpret a diagonal entry as retained coordinate energy. For an orthogonal projector, pii=‖Pei‖2. Thus it lies between zero and one; the sum of all such entries is the integer rank.

Decision 26

Exploit endpoint diagonal values. A zero diagonal entry forces the corresponding row and column to vanish. A diagonal entry one forces that coordinate direction to be fixed with every other entry in its row and column zero.

Decision 27

Use both off-diagonal bounds. For distinct indices, pij2≤piipjj and pij2≤(1-pii)(1-pjj). These come from the projector and its complement. They are necessary tests, not a complete existence theorem.

Decision 28

Do not replace a matrix identity by its diagonal. Bounds and integer trace can reject impossible candidates, but a matrix passing them may still fail idempotence. Off-diagonal equations can impose indispensable sign or magnitude conditions.

Decision 29

Transform the metric under nonorthonormal coordinates. If x=Bz, the coordinate metric is BTB. The coordinate projector is B-1PB and satisfies metric self-adjointness even when ordinary symmetry is absent.

Decision 30

Use the correct weighted normal direction. For constraint row D in metric G, the correction is in the span of G-1DT. Using DT instead generally solves the Euclidean problem rather than the weighted one.

Decision 31

Keep positive definiteness as a real premise. A positive-semidefinite form can assign zero cost to a nonzero direction, so closest points may not be unique. A singular metric cannot be substituted into an inverse formula derived for a norm without a separate argument.

Decision 32

Preserve every complex conjugation. For complex vectors, use u*u, not uTu. The latter can vanish for a nonzero vector such as (1,i)T. A convention difference in which argument is linear must be translated consistently.

Combine subspaces only with justified hypotheses

Decision 33

Check commutation before calling a product a projection. For orthogonal projectors, PQ is an orthogonal projector exactly when PQ=QP. In that case its range is the intersection. Without commutation, neither symmetry nor idempotence is automatic.

Decision 34

Use sums for perpendicular ranges. The plain sum P+Q is a projector exactly when PQ=0 for orthogonal projectors. Overlapping directions would otherwise be counted twice. Perpendicular ranges are stronger than merely having zero intersection.

Decision 35

Use the corrected sum for commuting overlap. When the projectors commute, P+Q-PQ projects onto the sum of the ranges. The subtraction removes their intersection. Without commutation, the expression can be nonsymmetric and wrong.

Decision 36

Respect the sign of a contained-space difference. If the range of P lies inside the range of Q, then Q-P projects onto the part added by Q. The reverse difference acts by minus one there and is generally not a projection.

Decision 37

Treat product trace as overlap, not an integer dimension. The value tr(PQ)=‖PQ‖F2 is nonnegative and may be fractional. For line projectors it is the squared cosine of the angle. It equals an intersection dimension in the commuting case.

Decision 38

Use trace bounds with ambient dimension. For ranks r,s in dimension m, max(0,r+s-m)≤tr(PQ)≤min(r,s). The lower bound uses the unavoidable intersection and nonnegative contributions from other directions.

Decision 39

Use saturation to prove containment. If tr(PQ)=rank(P), every unit basis vector of the range of P must retain all its energy under Q. Thus that range is contained in the range of Q. The argument requires orthogonal positivity.

Decision 40

Compare projectors through a matrix distance. The identity ‖P-Q‖F2=r+s-2tr(PQ) compares subspaces, not signed vector representatives. Changing a line's generator to its negative does not change its projector or this distance.

Distinguish finite algorithms from exact operators

Decision 41

Name the reflection convention. This chapter uses H=2P-I, which fixes the range and negates its perpendicular complement. The alternative I-2P reflects across the complementary space. Both square to the identity but fix different directions.

Decision 42

Use symmetry when recovering a projector from a reflection. If H is symmetric and orthogonal, (I+H)/2 is an orthogonal projector. An arbitrary orthogonal rotation does not satisfy this conclusion because its square need not be the identity.

Decision 43

Count alternating-projection cycles consistently. A full cycle PQ applies Q first and then P. A display counting each application separately uses two steps per cycle. Reversing this convention changes the reported finite trajectory.

Decision 44

Do not label a finite iterate as its limit. Distinct nonperpendicular lines have zero intersection, but repeated projection can remain nonzero after every finite cycle. Its limit is zero. A simulation should show the finite vector and its convergence factor explicitly.

Decision 45

Handle limiting angles before using logarithms. The cycle count for two distinct acute lines uses a logarithm of a cosine strictly between zero and one. Perpendicular lines finish in one cycle, while coincident lines have a different intersection and no such decay formula.

Decision 46

Keep rank-change examples separate from fixed-rank stability. Generator matrices can converge while their column spaces drop rank at the limit. The limiting projector need not equal the projector of the limiting matrix. The example does not refute continuity on a fixed-rank neighborhood.

Decision 47

Prefer applying an orthonormal basis over building a dense matrix. Compute Q(QTb) directly when the basis is available. This retains exact geometric meaning and uses storage proportional to the basis size rather than the ambient matrix size.

Decision 48

Do not equate mathematical formulas with stable code. Normal equations square the full-column-rank spectral condition number. QR can avoid that additional squaring in the algorithm, but cannot remove intrinsic sensitivity or infer an undeclared numerical rank.

Decision 49

Separate fitted-vector uniqueness from coefficient uniqueness. A deficient generator matrix still has one physical closest point. Its coefficient minimizers differ by nullspace vectors. Only the minimum-norm one is perpendicular to the coefficient nullspace.

Decision 50

Finish with an independent check. Verify feasibility, residual perpendicularity, dimensions and an energy or direct-distance calculation. Agreement of these different certificates catches sign, normalization and space-selection errors that repeated multiplication of the same mistaken formula may miss.

Editable geometry laboratory

Choose an angle, input coordinates and a positive vertical weight. Every run begins paused. Coordinate arrows are drawn in an ordinary coordinate plane; when the weight differs from one, the perpendicularity certificate uses the declared weighted product. The display rounds decimals to four places; it does not assert exact decimal arithmetic.
